description_full: Kite Realty Group Trust is a real estate investment trust (REIT) that owns and operates a high-quality portfolio of open-air shopping centers and mixed-use destinations. The Company's portfolio is concentrated in high-growth Sun Belt and select strategic gateway markets. KRG has more than six decades of experience in developing, operating, and investing in real estate, using a disciplined, hands-on approach to enhance portfolio quality and maximize long-term value for all stakeholders. As of September 30, 2026, the Company owned interests in 164 U.S. open-air shopping centers and mixed-use assets, comprising approximately 26.3 million square feet of gross leasable space. Kite Realty Group Trust was incorporated in 1971 in Maryland and based in Indianapolis.
ceo_bio: Mr. John A. Kite | Chairman of the Board of Trustees & CEO | Age 59 | Compensation: $4.0M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 228 people. Revenue per employee of $3.7M ranks in the above the sector median among Real Estate peers, improving at 16%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $1.2M of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $47K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Kite Realty Group Trust is a mid-cap real estate business with a $5.2B market cap on $844M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 1% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $278M in free cash flow — roughly 33 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.44× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 7.9× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 3.3×.

Shareholder yield of 4.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+46.4% a year).

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 14% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 18% and a beta of 0.81, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.00 vs 5y 0.78), so read it loosely.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $19.69 (margin of safety -29%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 11%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $11.64 to $32.16 (P10-P90).

The price implies 5.6% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 1% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.3%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.49).
It converts 33% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.44x.

hlth: Leverage is heavy at 7.9x net debt to EBITDA ($36.8M of cash against $3.0B of debt), with interest covered 3.3x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.69 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.7% over 3 years, 25.9% over 5 years and 9.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 39%).
Free cash flow has compounded 37.1% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 35.1% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (18.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 58, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 40.8% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.8%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 4.6% a year to shareholders (0.0% in buybacks and 4.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 21 consecutive years, raising it 44.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 228 employees, each generates about $3.7M of revenue, 1.6x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 16.3% a year.
That works out to $1.2M of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.0M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
